planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the glossy, dark green foliage stays especially handsome even when not in bloom.

directions: Set crowns with the rhizome tip just below the soil surface in rich, evenly moist soil enriched with compost. Irrlicht produces slightly fragrant, densely packed white plumes over a tidy mound of glossy, deeply cut dark green foliage that reads noticeably darker than most Arendsii cultivars, making it a strong contrast plant among pink and red astilbes. Keep soil consistently moist through summer heat, since foliage scorches and browns quickly if it dries out, and give it a bit of morning sun to encourage the densest flowering. Divide every three to four years in spring when clumps become congested to keep bloom vigorous.

common_name: Red Sentinel Astilbe (Scarlet-Plumed Arendsii False Goatsbeard)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; bronze-red spring foliage and mahogany stems add color even before bloom.

directions: Plant crowns shallowly in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to light shade, where mahogany-red stems carry scarlet plumes above a mound of ferny leaves. Foliage emerges coppery bronze in spring before deepening to dark green, giving Red Sentinel strong seasonal interest beyond its late-spring bloom. Mulch and irrigate through summer dry spells, since astilbe foliage browns rapidly once soil moisture drops, and leave spent plumes standing for winter texture and cut-flower use. Lift and divide crowded clumps in spring every three to four years to sustain strong flowering.

common_name: Montgomery Astilbe (Dark Magenta-Red Japonica Hybrid Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; avoid afternoon sun, which can scorch the glossy bronze-red new growth.

directions: Set crowns just below the soil surface in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, sheltering plants from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the new growth. Montgomery bears dense, dark magenta-red plumes on upright dark red stems above glossy, deep green fern-like foliage that emerges bronze-red in spring, and the spent plumes fade to an attractive caramel color that carries winter interest. Keep the root zone consistently moist with a organic mulch layer, since this heavy-shade-tolerant cultivar still needs steady moisture to perform well. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to renew vigor and bloom density.
